hits.title: Mycenaean Painted Stirrup Jar, Argolid Greece
hits.description: Aegean, Greece, Mycenaean. A broad-shouldered vessel of buff terracotta whose ingenious plumbing announces its purpose: a solid false neck capped by a disc, flanked by two arching strap handles, with the true spout set apart on the shoulder so that precious liquid could be poured in a controlled trickle and stoppered without loss. Encircling bands of lustrous brown slip sweep across the depressed globular body, gathering density toward the base, while the shoulder carries chevron-like curvilinear arcs with hatched edging. Stirrup jars of this form were the standard shipping container of the Mycenaean world, carrying perfumed oil and wine from Argolid workshops across the Aegean and into Egypt and the Levant. Their design is functional poetry, engineered for sealing, stacking, and the long haul of maritime trade. The stirrup jar (Greek pseudostomos amphoreus, "false-mouthed amphora") is the type fossil of Late Helladic commerce. Linear B tablets from Knossos and Pylos record the oil industry these vessels served, and inscribed coarse-ware examples found at Thebes and in Cyprus preserve place names and personal names in the same script, making the humble container one of the few Bronze Age objects that occasionally speaks. Argolid workshops around Mycenae and Berbati were the dominant exporters, and their products turn up from Sardinia to Ugarit, tracing the reach of a palace economy that vanished with the collapse of the twelfth century BCE. In 1915, he entered into a landmark exclusive collaboration with the premier American fashion magazine Harper's Bazar (now known as Harper's Bazaar after a name change in 1929/1930), a prolific creative partnership that famously spanned over two decades. Between 1915 and 1936, Erté shaped the visual landscape of modern luxury by designing over 240 covers and providing hundreds of interior fashion illustrations for the publication. The original production stamp preserved on the verso of the present lot details its preparation for the June 1925 issue. Received and processed by the editorial offices on 28 April 1925, the piece is recorded under inventory tracking number 43, registering its place in the publication's layout sequence.
